from an averaging truth probe, does a max-pooled probe still catch them?
Answer: Not settled, because only two of three planned runs finished.
shared_label: same score in the true sentence
foot: Alarm line: 1% of true statements cross it. Dots: fine-tune 1 of 2. Percentages: 596 false statements.
Source: kran-research max-pool-8b · Kran Lab, Nov 20, 2026 · blog.kran.ai/lab
alt: Figure 1. Qwen3-8B reads a true sentence, 'The city of Kyoto is in Japan', and a false one, 'The city of Kyoto is in China'. A max-pooled truth probe scores every word and rings if its highest score crosses an alarm line that 1% of true statements cross. In the original model, 'China' scores far above the line, and the probe catches {main_clean} of 596 false statements. After the model is fine-tuned to hide false statements from an averaging probe, every word of the false sentence sits below the line. The highest word is now 'Kyoto', which scores the same in the true sentence. The probe then catches {main_pooled} ({main_s0} and {main_s1} in the two runs that finished; a third planned run had not). In Qwen2.5-1.5B the same fine-tune took it from {ref_clean} to {ref_pooled}. A fine-tune pushed along a random direction leaves it at {ctrl_s0} and {ctrl_s1}. The answer is not settled, because only two of three planned runs finished.
notes: Qwen2.5-1.5B (earlier post): {ref_clean} before, {ref_pooled} after the same fine-tune.
Same fine-tune pushed along a random direction: {ctrl_s0} and {ctrl_s1} still caught.
